title: Let Us Praise the Fathers
sum: Ben Sira turns from God's works in nature (42–43) to God's works in Israel's history. He opens a long hymn in praise of 'the fathers': rulers, counselors, prophets, scribes, poets and rich men whose names live on, while others vanish as if they had never been (44:1–15). Their glory is God's gift, and it lasts through their children and the covenants.

Then the roll call begins. Enoch, carried off by God, is a pattern for later generations; Noah is the new start after the flood; Abraham keeps the law, is circumcised and passes the test, and receives God's oath; the blessing passes to Isaac and Jacob and the twelve tribes, and from them comes Moses (44:16–23). The Hebrew manuscript B calls these 'men of loyal love' (hesed), and the Masada scroll, the oldest copy, lacks the verse on Enoch.
readings: Read as history
Ben Sira retells Genesis closely, adding little. His interest is the line of covenants that leads from Noah and Abraham to Israel's priests and kings, the institutions of his own Jerusalem.
Read as teaching
The hymn is a lesson for students: live so that your name is remembered with blessing. Fame comes from faithfulness (44:10), not from wealth or power alone.

views.C: Catholic Bibles, following the Council of Trent's list (1546), include Ecclesiasticus. The Latin Vulgate's text of 44:16 adds that Enoch was carried off 'into paradise', a detail that fed later Christian reflection on where Enoch and Elijah were kept.
views.O: The Orthodox Old Testament is the Septuagint, so the Greek text translated here, with its 'example of repentance' for Enoch, is the text Orthodox readers know.
views.P: Protestants place Sirach among the Apocrypha. The Church of England's Article VI says such books are read 'for example of life and instruction of manners', and the Praise of the Fathers is that kind of reading: a roll of examples, like Hebrews 11.
views.H: Historians read 44–50 as a carefully built composition, not a list. Ben Sira chooses and shapes his heroes to lead to Simon the high priest (50:1–21). The Masada scroll shows the Hebrew text circulating within two centuries of the author.
views.J: The Hebrew title, 'Praise of the fathers of old', and the phrase 'men of loyal love' make the hymn a Jewish meditation on the covenant fathers. Its order follows the Torah and then the Prophets, the order of the Jewish Bible.

deep.h: The plan of the Praise of the Fathers
deep.b:
After an opening hymn (44:1–15) Ben Sira moves through the Torah (Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, Phinehas: 44:16–45:26), the Former Prophets (Joshua, Caleb, the judges, Samuel, Nathan, David, Solomon, Rehoboam, Jeroboam, Elijah, Elisha, Hezekiah: 46:1–48:25) and the Latter Prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, the Twelve: 48:20–49:10), then the return from exile (Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah: 49:11–13). He turns back to the first humans (Enoch, Joseph, Shem, Seth, Adam: 49:14–16) and ends with Simon son of Onias (50:1–21). The order shows that by about 180 BC the Law and the Prophets were already a known sequence of books, a point Ben Sira's grandson makes in his prologue.

Some are missing: Ezra (see 49:13), Daniel, Esther, and all the women of Israel's story. Priests get the most space: Aaron alone has seventeen verses.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a hymn that ends in the temple
deep.b: This is my own reading, though it overlaps with what many commentators observe. Ben Sira's list begins with Enoch, who 'walked with God', and climbs through covenants of priesthood (Aaron, 45:7; Phinehas, 45:24) toward the high priest in the temple (50:1–21). Wisdom in chapter 24 also travels from creation to a resting place in the temple in Zion (24:8–12). So the two great hymns of the book may be meant to match: Wisdom finds her home in the sanctuary, and the history of the fathers finds its goal in the priest who serves there. On this reading, Simon is the living picture of Wisdom at home in Israel (compare 50:6–10 with 24:13–17).

echoes: Genesis 5:24; Genesis 6:9; Genesis 9:8–17; Genesis 17:5; Genesis 22:16–18; Genesis 26:5; Psalm 72:8; 1 Maccabees 2:51–60; Hebrews 11:1–40; Hebrews 11:5; Romans 4:9–17; James 2:21–23

settings.what: The opening of the Hymn of the Fathers
settings.by: Jesus son of Sirach (Ben Sira), the teacher
settings.to: his students and the 'assembly' that will tell the fathers' praise (44:15): Jerusalem's young men of the scribal class
settings.when: as the last great section of his book, after the hymn on God's works in creation (42:15–43:33)
settings.why: To show his students that God's glory is seen in faithful people as well as in nature, and to set before them models whose memory is blessed. A teacher of future leaders is telling them what kind of name to leave.
settings.readers: Ben Sira taught in Jerusalem about 180 BC, under the Seleucid kings, in the years after Antiochus III took Judea from Egypt (Josephus, Antiquities 12.138–141) and while Simon's family still held the high priesthood. His first hearers were young men of the scribal class (51:23). His grandson brought the book to Egypt in 132 BC and translated it there for Greek-speaking Jews (prologue). Hebrew copies were read at Masada before AD 73, and medieval copies were found in the Cairo Genizah from 1896.

settings.what: The roll call of the fathers, from Enoch to Adam
settings.to: his students, and through the book any Jewish reader
settings.when: about 180 BC, when the Law and the Prophets were already read as a set of books
settings.why: To retell Israel's history as a chain of covenants and faithful leaders, leading up to the priesthood and temple of his own day (50:1–21). It teaches that God keeps covenant with the fathers' children.
settings.readers: The first hearers knew these stories from the Torah and the Prophets. For the grandson's readers in Egypt after 132 BC, a minority among Greeks, the list was a proud account of their people's past in Greek dress; similar lists appear in 1 Maccabees 2:51–60 and, later, in Hebrews 11.

title: Moses, Aaron and Phinehas
sum: Moses, loved by God and people, receives the law face to face (45:1–5). Then Ben Sira gives Aaron more space than anyone except Simon: God makes an everlasting covenant with him, dresses him in splendid vestments, gives him the daily offerings, the blessing in God's name, the power to teach the law, and the firstfruits and sacrifices for his living, since the Lord himself is his inheritance (45:6–22). Korah's revolt only confirms Aaron's right (45:18–19).

Phinehas, third in glory, receives the covenant of peace and the priesthood forever for his zeal (45:23–24). Ben Sira sets David's royal covenant beside Aaron's (45:25) and ends with a blessing on the priests of his own day (45:26).
readings: Read for the priesthood
The chapter is a charter for the temple priests: their vestments, sacrifices, teaching role and income all come from God's covenant with Aaron and Phinehas.
Read as Scripture retold
Ben Sira stitches together Exodus 28–29, Leviticus 8–9, Numbers 16, 18 and 25, choosing the details that honor Aaron's line.

views.C: Catholic readers have long seen in Aaron's ordination, anointing and blessing a figure of the Christian priesthood; that question is the card at Exodus 28.
views.O: The Orthodox Church reads the Greek text, in which Aaron's covenant is 'a covenant that lasts forever' and the vestments are 'garments of might'.
views.P: Protestant readers, who stress the one priesthood of Christ (Hebrews 7), read the chapter as history of Israel's worship and as a type of Christ, not as a pattern for church ministers.
views.H: Historians see the outlook of a Jerusalem scribe close to the temple aristocracy. The Hebrew of 45:24 gives Phinehas's line 'the high priesthood forever', which supports the claims of the Zadokite family to which Simon belonged.
views.J: The Mishnah tells disciples to be like the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace (Mishnah Avot 1:12). Manuscript B's call 'And now bless the LORD, the good one' shows the hymn being used in worship.

echoes: Exodus 4:16; Exodus 20:21; Exodus 28:1–43; Exodus 29:38–42; Exodus 33:11; Leviticus 2:2; Leviticus 6:20; Leviticus 8:1–36; Numbers 6:27; Numbers 12:3–7; Numbers 16:1–35; Numbers 18:20; Numbers 25:6–13; Malachi 2:5; Psalm 106:30–31; 1 Maccabees 2:26; 1 Maccabees 2:54; Hebrews 7:11–17

settings.to: the priests of the Jerusalem temple in his day, Aaron's heirs (the 'you' is plural)
settings.when: at the end of the section on Aaron and Phinehas; manuscript B first calls them to 'bless the LORD, the good one, who crowns you with glory'
settings.why: To pray that the priests, who judged and taught the people, would have wisdom to rule rightly so that their glory would last. It ties Israel's history to the living priesthood of Simon's house.
settings.readers: For the first hearers the priests were Jerusalem's leaders, with no king. For the grandson's readers in Egypt, Simon's line had already lost the office (see 50:24), so the blessing read as a prayer for priests in general.

title: Joshua, Caleb, the Judges and Samuel
sum: Joshua, Moses' successor in prophecy and a savior true to his name, fights the Lord's wars: the sun stands back, hail falls on the enemy, and with Caleb he stays faithful when the spies' report sets the people grumbling. The two alone of six hundred thousand enter the land, and Caleb keeps his strength into old age (46:1–10).

The faithful judges are blessed as a group, with a wish that their bones may sprout again (46:11–12). Samuel, prophet and judge, sets up the kingdom, offers a nursing lamb when the Philistines attack, and the Lord thunders; before his death he swears he took no bribe, and after his death he still prophesies to Saul (46:13–20).
readings: Read as a story of faithfulness
Each hero 'followed fully after' the Lord: Joshua and Caleb in the wilderness, the judges whose hearts stayed true, Samuel who took nothing from anyone.
Read with the Hebrew
Manuscript B adds color the Greek lacks: Joshua's javelin, the 'wars of the LORD', 'every nation of the ban', and Samuel as 'Nazirite, judge and priest'.

views.C: For Catholics, whose Bible includes both Sirach and 2 Maccabees, 46:20 stands beside 2 Maccabees 15:12–14, where the dead high priest Onias and Jeremiah pray for Israel; whether the faithful dead can hear or help the living is the card at 1 Samuel 28.
views.O: Orthodox readers know Joshua by his Greek name Iēsous and have long read him as a type of Jesus, who leads God's people into rest.
views.P: Protestant readers compare Ben Sira's heroes with the list in Hebrews 11:30–32 and note that Hebrews praises their faith, where Ben Sira praises their faithfulness and zeal.
views.H: Ben Sira takes 1 Samuel 28 as a real appearance of Samuel and Joshua 10 as a real standing of the sun. Historians read the chapter as evidence of how these texts were understood about 180 BC.
views.J: Ben Sira's honoring of the judges 'each by his own name' recalls the Jewish custom of blessing the memory of the righteous dead.

echoes: Exodus 33:11; Numbers 13:30; Numbers 14:6–38; Joshua 8:18; Joshua 10:11–14; Joshua 14:6–15; Judges 2:16–19; Judges 8:27; 1 Samuel 7:5–11; 1 Samuel 12:1–5; 1 Samuel 28:3–25; Isaiah 66:14; Matthew 1:21; Hebrews 4:8; Hebrews 11:30–32

settings.by: Samuel, as Ben Sira retells him
settings.to: all Israel, gathered before the Lord and his anointed king Saul (1 Samuel 12)
settings.when: at the end of Samuel's leadership, 'before he lay down in his everlasting sleep'
settings.why: Inside the story, Samuel clears his name before handing over to the king. For Ben Sira's students, who would serve as judges and officials, it is a model of the honest leader who takes no bribe (compare 20:29).
settings.readers: Ben Sira taught in Jerusalem about 180 BC, under the Seleucid kings, in the years after Antiochus III took Judea from Egypt (Josephus, Antiquities 12.138–141) and while Simon's family still held the high priesthood. His first hearers were young men of the scribal class (51:23). His grandson brought the book to Egypt in 132 BC and translated it there for Greek-speaking Jews (prologue). Hebrew copies were read at Masada before AD 73, and medieval copies were found in the Cairo Genizah from 1896.

title: Nathan, David and Solomon
sum: Nathan prophesies in David's day (47:1). David, chosen out of Israel like the fat of the offering, plays with lions, kills Goliath, wins his tens of thousands, crushes the Philistines, sings to God with all his heart, sets up the temple singers and festivals, and is forgiven and given a covenant of kings (47:2–11).

Solomon reigns in peace and builds the house, and his wisdom, songs and proverbs fill the earth; but he heaps up gold and gives himself to women, and the kingdom splits (47:12–21). Yet God keeps a remnant and a root for David (47:22). Rehoboam, 'the folly of the people', and Jeroboam, who made Israel sin, lead the people to ruin (47:23–25).
readings: Read as a portrait of kingship

David is the ideal king as Chronicles paints him: warrior, singer and founder of worship. Solomon shows how wisdom and wealth can still fail when a king breaks Deuteronomy's law for kings (Deuteronomy 17:16–17).
Read for hope
Despite Solomon's sin, God will never wipe out David's line (47:22). Jewish and Christian readers have found in this 'root' the hope of a Messiah.

views.C: Catholic tradition reads the 'root' of David (47:22) with Isaiah 11 as fulfilled in Christ, the Son of David.
views.O: Orthodox worship sings the Psalms of David daily, and Ben Sira's picture of David as the founder of temple song fits that use.
views.P: Protestant commentators note how frankly Ben Sira names Solomon's sins, as Kings does, and read 47:22 as testimony to God's faithfulness to his promise.
views.H: Ben Sira's David depends on Chronicles (the singers, the festivals) as well as Samuel. His blunt judgment on Solomon follows 1 Kings 11 and Deuteronomy 17.
views.J: Manuscript B's pun on Rehoboam ('broad in folly') and its curse on Jeroboam's memory are typical of Hebrew wordplay lost in the Greek.

echoes: 2 Samuel 7:12–16; 2 Samuel 12:13; 1 Samuel 17:34–51; 1 Samuel 18:7; 1 Chronicles 16:4–7; 1 Chronicles 22:9; 1 Chronicles 25:1–31; 1 Kings 4:29–34; 1 Kings 10:1–27; 1 Kings 11:1–13; 1 Kings 12:1–33; 1 Kings 14:16; Deuteronomy 17:16–17; Isaiah 11:1–10; Romans 15:12

settings.by: Ben Sira, speaking to the long-dead king
settings.to: Solomon, as if present; really Ben Sira's students
settings.when: in the middle of the hymn, after Solomon's peaceful reign is described
settings.why: Turning to speak to Solomon ('How wise you grew...') makes the lesson personal: the wisest of kings fell through wealth and women. Students who hoped for wisdom and position are warned that neither protects a man who breaks God's law.
settings.readers: Ben Sira taught in Jerusalem about 180 BC, under the Seleucid kings, in the years after Antiochus III took Judea from Egypt (Josephus, Antiquities 12.138–141) and while Simon's family still held the high priesthood. His first hearers were young men of the scribal class (51:23). His grandson brought the book to Egypt in 132 BC and translated it there for Greek-speaking Jews (prologue). Hebrew copies were read at Masada before AD 73, and medieval copies were found in the Cairo Genizah from 1896.

title: Elijah, Elisha, Hezekiah and Isaiah
sum: Elijah rises like fire: he shuts the sky, calls down fire three times, raises the dead, brings kings down, hears God at Horeb, anoints kings and prophets, and is carried up in a whirlwind of fire. Ben Sira, addressing him, says he is 'written down' to return before God's anger breaks out, to turn fathers' hearts and restore the tribes of Jacob (48:1–11), the promise of Malachi 4:5–6.

Elisha, filled with his spirit, fears no ruler, and even his dead body brings a man back to life (48:12–14). The people still do not repent and are scattered (48:15–16). Hezekiah brings water into Jerusalem through the rock; when Sennacherib threatens Zion, the people pray, Isaiah answers, and the angel strikes the Assyrian camp; the sun goes back, and Isaiah sees the last things and comforts Zion's mourners (48:17–25).
readings: Read as prophecy fulfilled
For Christians, Elijah's promised return points to John the Baptist (Luke 1:17; Matthew 17:10–13). Ben Sira shows that the hope was alive two centuries earlier.
Read as history
The chapter retells Kings faithfully, with details that match the record: Hezekiah's tunnel still exists in Jerusalem.

views.C: Catholic readers cite 48:13–14 with 2 Kings 13:21 in the discussion of relics (card at 2 Kings 13), and read 48:10 with Luke 1:17 of John the Baptist.
views.O: The Orthodox Church honors Elijah as a living prophet who did not die. Ben Sira's 'taken up in a whirlwind of fire' and 'written down for the times to come' fit that devotion; where he went is the card at 2 Kings 2.
views.P: Protestant readers often cite 48:10 as evidence that Malachi's promise of Elijah was understood before Christ, and read its fulfillment in John the Baptist (Matthew 11:14).
views.H: 48:24 shows that by about 180 BC the whole book of Isaiah, including chapters 40–66, was read as Isaiah's. 48:10 is the earliest use of Malachi outside the prophets, which shows the Prophets were a fixed collection by then.
views.J: Jewish tradition gave Elijah a central place as the herald of the Messiah; the cup of Elijah at the Passover table and the chair of Elijah at a circumcision come from that hope. Ben Sira's 'to set the tribes of Jacob on their feet' gives him the task of gathering Israel.

echoes: 1 Kings 17:1–24; 1 Kings 18:38; 1 Kings 19:8–19; 2 Kings 1:2–17; 2 Kings 2:1–15; 2 Kings 13:20–21; 2 Kings 17:7–23; 2 Kings 18:13–20:21; Isaiah 36–39; Isaiah 40:1; Isaiah 49:6; Isaiah 61:2–3; Malachi 4:5–6; Luke 1:17; Matthew 17:10–13; James 5:17

settings.by: Ben Sira, speaking to the prophet
settings.to: Elijah, as if present; really Ben Sira's students
settings.why: Speaking straight to Elijah ('How glorious you were') turns history into hope: Elijah is not only a figure of the past but 'written down' to return. Ben Sira's hearers, under foreign rule, are told that God has a messenger ready to restore Israel.
settings.readers: Ben Sira taught in Jerusalem about 180 BC, under the Seleucid kings, in the years after Antiochus III took Judea from Egypt (Josephus, Antiquities 12.138–141) and while Simon's family still held the high priesthood. His first hearers were young men of the scribal class (51:23). His grandson brought the book to Egypt in 132 BC and translated it there for Greek-speaking Jews (prologue). Hebrew copies were read at Masada before AD 73, and medieval copies were found in the Cairo Genizah from 1896. Christians read the passage beside Luke 1:17, where the angel applies Malachi's words to John the Baptist.

title: Josiah, the Prophets and the Builders
sum: Josiah's memory is sweet as incense and honey; he turned the people back and made godliness strong in lawless times (49:1–3). Apart from David, Hezekiah and Josiah, the kings of Judah sinned, gave their glory to foreigners, and the city burned, because of what they did to Jeremiah, the prophet made holy in the womb (49:4–7).

Ezekiel sees the chariot of glory (49:8–9; manuscript B names Job here). May the bones of the Twelve Prophets sprout, for they comforted Jacob (49:10). Zerubbabel the seal ring and Jeshua the priest rebuild the house; Nehemiah raises the walls (49:11–13). Ezra is not named. Then the hymn reaches back: Enoch, Joseph, Shem and Seth, and Adam above all creation (49:14–16).
readings: Read for the canon
Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and 'the Twelve Prophets' come in the order of the Hebrew Bible's Latter Prophets. 49:10 is the oldest known mention of the Twelve as a group.
Read for the omissions
No Ezra, no Daniel, no Esther: the list is a chosen story, aimed at builders and priests.

views.C: Catholic and Orthodox Bibles follow the Greek here, which lacks Job; the Latin agrees with the Greek ('inimicorum').
views.O: Orthodox readers note Jeshua's Greek name, Iēsous, and the Christian reading of Zechariah's 'two sons of oil' (Zechariah 4:14) as king and priest.
views.P: Protestant readers interested in the canon cite 49:10 for the Twelve and the Prophets as a recognized collection before Christ.
views.H: Scholars use 49:10 as early evidence for the Book of the Twelve. The silence about Ezra has been explained in several ways; none is certain.
views.J: Manuscript B's 'and he also mentioned Job the prophet' (49:9) agrees with the Jewish view that Job was a real figure; the Greek lost the name by reading 'enemy'.

echoes: 2 Kings 22:1–23:30; 2 Kings 23:25; Jeremiah 1:5; Jeremiah 1:10; Ezekiel 1:4–28; Ezekiel 14:14; Haggai 2:23; Ezra 3:2; Zechariah 4:14; Nehemiah 2:17; Genesis 5:24; Genesis 50:25; Genesis 4:25–26; Romans 5:12

title: Simon the High Priest
sum: The hymn reaches its goal in Ben Sira's own day: Simon son of Onias, the high priest, who repaired the temple, built its walls and reservoir and strengthened Jerusalem against siege (50:1–4). Ben Sira paints him coming out from the house of the curtain, shining like the morning star, the moon, the sun and the rainbow, like roses, lilies, cedars, olive and cypress (50:5–10).

At the altar, robed in splendor and ringed by his brother priests, he offers the sacrifice and pours the wine; the priests blow trumpets, the people fall on their faces, the singers praise, and Simon comes down and blesses the people in the Lord's name (50:11–21). Ben Sira calls all to bless God (50:22–24), names three nations he loathes (50:25–26), and signs his book (50:27–29).
readings: Read as eyewitness
This is the only description of the temple service by someone who saw it, written about 180 BC. It is close to what the Mishnah, compiled about AD 200, describes for the daily offering.
Read as the climax of the hymn
The high priest in Aaron's robes (compare 45:8 and 50:11) is the living result of God's covenants with the fathers.

views.C: Ecclesiasticus is part of the Catholic canon. Christian readers can set the high priest who comes out to bless the people beside Hebrews, where Christ the high priest appears a second time to save those who wait for him (Hebrews 9:11–12, 28).
views.O: The Orthodox Church reads this chapter in the Greek, where the high priest's vestments are the 'robe of glory' and 'the fullness of splendor' of Aaron (45:7–8).
views.P: Lutherans sing 50:22–24 in Rinkart's 'Now Thank We All Our God'. Protestant readers, while not treating Sirach as Scripture, value the chapter for its picture of temple worship before Christ.
views.H: Historians identify Simon with Simon II, about 200 BC, and connect his building work with Antiochus III's decree (Josephus, Antiquities 12.138–141). Whether the scene is the Day of Atonement or the daily offering is debated (see 50:5).
views.J: The Mishnah's tractate Tamid (7:2–3) describes much the same service, and the Yom Kippur poem 'Mareh Kohen' echoes Ben Sira's picture of the high priest. Jewish tradition remembers 'Shimon the Righteous' (Mishnah Avot 1:2).

deep.h: Day of Atonement or daily offering?
deep.b: Readers have long asked which service Ben Sira describes. For the Day of Atonement: Simon comes out 'from the house of the curtain' (50:5), and only on that day did the high priest go behind the inner curtain (Leviticus 16; Mishnah Yoma 5:1); the people's falling on their faces recalls Yoma 6:2; and the synagogue's Yom Kippur poetry later borrowed this chapter. For the daily offering (Tamid): the details of 50:12–21 match Mishnah Tamid 7:3 point by point, the pieces handed up, the libation, two trumpets, the Levites' song and the people bowing, and Tamid 7:2 for the blessing; and there is no scapegoat, incense in the inner room or sprinkled blood. A third view is that Ben Sira blends what he saw on many days into one picture.

echoes: Exodus 28:2; Exodus 29:38–42; Leviticus 9:22; Leviticus 16:1–34; Numbers 6:22–27; Numbers 10:1–10; Deuteronomy 32:21; 1 Kings 7:23–26; 2 Chronicles 29:26–30; Psalm 133:2; 2 Maccabees 3:1; 2 Maccabees 4:34; John 4:9; Hebrews 9:7; Mishnah Tamid 7:2–3; Mishnah Avot 1:2

settings.what: The portrait of Simon at the altar
settings.to: his students and readers in Jerusalem, many of whom had seen Simon themselves
settings.when: probably after Simon's death, since the verbs look back on his lifetime (50:1); about 180 BC
settings.why: To crown the history of the fathers with the high priest of their own time, and to show that the glory of God's covenants was present in Jerusalem's temple. Knowing that the hearers had seen this changes the reading: it is memory, not legend.
settings.readers: Ben Sira taught in Jerusalem about 180 BC, under the Seleucid kings, in the years after Antiochus III took Judea from Egypt (Josephus, Antiquities 12.138–141) and while Simon's family still held the high priesthood. His first hearers were young men of the scribal class (51:23). His grandson brought the book to Egypt in 132 BC and translated it there for Greek-speaking Jews (prologue). Hebrew copies were read at Masada before AD 73, and medieval copies were found in the Cairo Genizah from 1896. For the grandson's readers after 132 BC Simon's family had lost the office, and Josephus says a son of Simon's son Onias founded a rival temple at Leontopolis in Egypt (see the topic page on Onias).
views: The coming out from behind the curtain points to Yom Kippur.
The details match Mishnah Tamid 7:2–3 for the daily burnt offering.

settings.what: The call to bless God and the prayer for Simon
settings.to: the worshipers ('all of you'), then God
settings.when: right after the description of the service
settings.why: To turn the picture into worship. In the Hebrew it prays that God's loyal love and the covenant of Phinehas stay with Simon's family; the Greek prays for 'us'.
settings.readers: The grandson's Greek readers after 132 BC prayed the general form. Centuries later the Lutheran Martin Rinkart made 50:22–24 into the hymn 'Now Thank We All Our God'.

settings.what: A saying about three hated nations
settings.when: as a short aside after the prayer
settings.why: To name Judea's neighbors as outsiders to the covenant: Edom (Seir in the Hebrew) or Samaria, the Philistine coast, and above all the Samaritans at Shechem with their temple on Mount Gerizim.
settings.readers: For first readers in Jerusalem the Samaritans were a near and bitter rival; the hostility still stood in Jesus' day (John 4:9).

settings.by: Jesus son of Sirach (Hebrew: Simeon son of Jeshua son of Eleazar son of Sira)
settings.when: at the end of the main body of the book
settings.why: To put his name to his teaching and promise that whoever lives by it will become wise. It is the only place the book names its author.
settings.readers: The grandson's prologue names his grandfather Jesus; these lines are where later readers took the book's names, 'Sirach' and 'Ben Sira'.

title: A Prayer, a Psalm and a Poem on Seeking Wisdom
sum: Ben Sira thanks God for rescuing him from slander before a king, from enemies, from fire and from the edge of Hades. When no one helped, he remembered God's mercy, called on 'the Father of my lord', and was heard (51:1–12). In the Hebrew manuscript B a litany follows, like Psalm 136, thanking God who gathers Israel, builds Zion, makes a horn sprout for David and chose the sons of Zadok as priests.

The book ends with an alphabet poem, also found in the Psalms Scroll from Qumran: as a youth he prayed for wisdom, followed her tracks, fought for her, and found her (51:13–22). Now he invites the untaught into his house of instruction: get wisdom without money, put your neck under her yoke, and find rest, as he did (51:23–30).
readings: Read as autobiography
The prayer and poem may tell Ben Sira's own story: a danger at court (51:6), a youth spent seeking wisdom, a school in Jerusalem.
Read as models
Both pieces use the stock language of thanksgiving psalms and wisdom poems, offered as patterns for students' own prayer and study.

views.C: Catholic readers have read the invitation of 51:23–27 together with Christ's 'Come to me' (Matthew 11:28–30). The Latin numbering of these verses differs from the Greek (the Vulgate runs to 51:38).
views.O: Orthodox readers hear in 'the Father of my lord' (51:10) the Father of the Lord Jesus, as the Greek allows.
views.P: Protestant scholars have studied 51:23–27 for the background of Matthew 11:28–30 and the picture of Jesus as Wisdom.
views.H: The acrostic's presence in 11QPs-a suggests it circulated on its own; some think it was added to Sirach. The Hebrew litany after 51:12 is in manuscript B only, and its line on 'the sons of Zadok' is used to argue for an early date.
views.J: Manuscript B's 'my house of study' (beit midrash, 51:23) uses the term later given to the Jewish study hall, and 'the yoke' of wisdom matches the rabbis' 'yoke of the Torah' (Mishnah Avot 3:5).

echoes: Psalm 18:4–6; Psalm 89:26; Psalm 110:1; Psalm 136:1–26; Psalm 148:14; Jonah 2:2; Isaiah 55:1; Proverbs 9:1–6; Jeremiah 6:16; Matthew 11:28–30; Luke 1:47; Mishnah Avot 3:5

settings.what: A prayer of thanks for rescue
settings.by: Jesus son of Sirach (the Greek title names him)
settings.to: God, overheard by his students and readers
settings.when: after a danger of death caused by slander before a king; when is not known
settings.why: To give thanks publicly, as the Psalms do, and to show students that the wise man prays and that God hears. Whether the danger was real or the language is conventional is debated (see 51:2).
settings.readers: Ben Sira taught in Jerusalem about 180 BC, under the Seleucid kings, in the years after Antiochus III took Judea from Egypt (Josephus, Antiquities 12.138–141) and while Simon's family still held the high priesthood. His first hearers were young men of the scribal class (51:23). His grandson brought the book to Egypt in 132 BC and translated it there for Greek-speaking Jews (prologue). Hebrew copies were read at Masada before AD 73, and medieval copies were found in the Cairo Genizah from 1896.
views: He tells of travels and dangers in 31:12–13; the slander to 'the king' could be a real accusation before a Ptolemaic or Seleucid ruler.
Every phrase has parallels in the Psalms, so the prayer may be a pattern rather than a record.

settings.what: The Hebrew litany of thanks (only in manuscript B)
settings.by: Ben Sira, or a later Hebrew writer whose psalm was copied here
settings.to: worshipers, in call-and-response form ('for his loyal love is forever')
settings.when: inserted after 51:12 in the medieval manuscript B; not in the Greek or Latin
settings.why: To call Israel to thank God for creation, for gathering the exiles, for Zion, for David's line and for the Zadokite priests.
settings.readers: Readers of the Hebrew in the Middle Ages, whose copy was found in the Cairo Genizah. Its date of composition is debated.

settings.what: The alphabet poem on seeking wisdom, with the invitation to the untaught
settings.by: the speaker of the book, Ben Sira (though some think the poem is older or separate)
settings.to: young men without schooling, invited into 'the house of instruction'
settings.when: as the last word of the book
settings.why: To recruit students: wisdom is free, close at hand, and rewards a little toil with great rest. Knowing that it was an invitation to a real school makes 'come to me' an advertisement as well as a poem.
settings.readers: The poem was read at Qumran in the Psalms Scroll (11QPs-a, first century) apart from the rest of Sirach, and later Christians read it beside Matthew 11:28–30.
